answer: At dawn, a crystal archive pays for retained replicas, not registered names. Each agent commits a key-specific encoding of the corpus; fresh random block audits demand short-deadline proofs tied to that commitment. A plume of aliases needs separately encoded replicas, since one stored copy must not answer proofs for every key. More rewards then cost additional disk capacity and upkeep. This relies on a sound proof-of-replication scheme and deadlines that make on-demand re-encoding impractical; ordinary hashes alone do not prevent shared storage or prove independent operators.
